analysis.one_liner: Bars credit card companies from raising your interest rate based on unrelated credit report information.
analysis.headline: The bill to stop credit card issuers from raising rates based on unrelated credit report information never received a committee vote and died when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Credit Reporting Act to stop credit card companies from raising a cardholder's interest rate — or taking away a low introductory rate — based on negative information in a credit report that had nothing to do with how that person paid their own credit card bill. Card issuers could still raise rates if the cardholder's own actions on that account justified it, and they would have to disclose this limit clearly to customers. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders — particularly people who pay their own card on time but whose rate gets raised anyway because of something else on their credit report, like a late payment to another lender, a drop in credit score, or a new loan application. All consumers with credit cards would benefit from the required clear disclosure of when their rate can change.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card holders facing surprise rate hikes

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits credit card issuers from using negative information in a consumer report to raise a card's annual percentage rate, or to remove or increase an introductory rate, for any reason other than the cardholder's own actions on that specific account [S2] [S3].

This targets the practice known as 'universal default' or 'bait and switch,' where a card company advertises a low rate, then raises it because of something unrelated to that card — a mechanism that can push a household's existing balances to a much higher rate they never agreed to when they took on the debt [S2] [S3].

Requires issuers to clearly and conspicuously describe this limit in any mandatory disclosure or statement to the consumer, so cardholders know rate changes must relate to their own account [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which would lose a way to reprice existing balances upward — card issuers used credit report information to raise rates on customers whose own accounts were in good standing, and the bill would cut off that revenue source.

drawbacks.text: Issuers price risk across their whole book, and blocking them from re-pricing based on a customer's overall credit profile could lead to higher starting rates for everyone, since companies would lose a tool for separating risky from safe borrowers after issuing a card.

The bill covers only rate increases triggered by information in a consumer report; issuers could still raise rates for other reasons — including notice-based changes to variable rates or new terms — so its real-world reach depends on how much universal-default repricing actually flowed through credit reports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For cardholders, the benefit is real and direct: it stops a documented practice of raising rates on existing balances for reasons unrelated to the card itself, protecting people who took on debt at one rate and suddenly owed far more at another. The cost falls on issuers, who argued risk-based repricing helps keep rates low for good customers; an honest reading is that this bill would shift some risk-pricing into initial rates. On balance it is a targeted consumer protection, though a narrow one — it regulates a single repricing channel rather than the whole practice of retroactive rate increases.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee — then a subcommittee — for the rest of the two-year Congress and never got a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on July 14, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S1] [S5].
Three weeks later, on August 4, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill drew 12 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4], and the committee never reported it to the House floor before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept the ability to raise rates on cardholders' existing balances based on unrelated credit report information, because the bill never advanced past a subcommittee referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers kept the status quo

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and championed it as its sole sponsor.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it sat at subcommittee referral until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was an Independent and all 12 cosponsors were Democrats; the Republican-controlled Financial Services Committee took no action beyond referral, and no vote was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would bar issuers from using negative credit report information to raise rates on existing balances unless the cardholder's own actions on that account justified it, eliminating a repricing tool for 'universal default' and intro-rate clawbacks. Card issuers profited by charging higher rates on debt customers had already taken on at a lower advertised rate.
Issuers buy credit report data to trigger rate increases; the bill restricts one profitable use of that data. The impact is modest, since bureaus sell reports for many other purposes.
